summary: The environment has the software and DocumentDB MCP data-plane tools needed to start building the Node.js unordered-bulk ingestion sample against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. Core developer tooling (Node/npx/npm), the documentdb MCP server, and Microsoft Learn documentation are present; the DocumentDB agent skills that guide index, driver and vector usage are installed. Several important cold answers from the model were out-of-date or confused this service with older Cosmos DB or other vendors; those must be corrected before producing code (notably: resource type / CLI group, billing model, connection-string host/port patterns, and vector/search support). Missing command-line clients (mongosh) and some IaC tools are not blocking but are worth adding or documenting workarounds.
summary_points: All runtime and agent skills needed to implement the Node.js sample are present: Node 24, npx, documentdb MCP server (data-plane), and the DocumentDB agent skills (driver, connection, indexing, vector-search, etc.).

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated — the service uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), the Azure CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster, billing is vCore/tiers (M-series) not RUs, and the service supports integrated vector and $search features.

Change streams, unordered bulkWrite, and compound-unique indexes are supported and documented for Azure DocumentDB; the sample can use collection.bulkWrite(..., { ordered: false }) and db.collection.createIndex(..., { unique: true }).
Missing developer tools (mongosh) and IaC CLIs (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are reported by inventory; only mongosh is worth adding to materially improve local verification.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps: the build can start, but the builder must apply the corrections listed below and may optionally install mongosh or document a mongosh-free verification path.
No required MCP server or skill is unavailable; Azure writes are disabled by policy, but the run environment already points to a pre-provisioned cluster so that restriction is not blocking.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Main resource type for a Cosmos/DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include databases and collections under that account).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters (the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible offering) use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older and different Azure offerings (Cosmos DB account resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts used by the Cosmos DB/RU API) share the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace, causing the model to answer with the Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' resource instead of the newer vCore 'mongoClusters' resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts resource type or the older CLI groups, IaC snippets and CLI commands would target the wrong resource and fail to deploy or manage the intended DocumentDB cluster (mongoClusters).
improvements: On the 'Quickstart: create a cluster' and 'Overview' pages, add a prominent note that the vCore-managed product uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the az documentdb mongocluster command group, distinguishing it from databaseAccounts-based Cosmos DB.
In agent kit docs (documentdb-mcp-setup), add the explicit mapping: "vCore clusters → Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; Cosmos DB (RU) → Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts".

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Core CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name <accountName> --resource-group <rg> --locations regionName='<region>' --kind MongoDB. This is part of the main azure-cli (not an extension).
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed mongoClusters) the CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create). The az cosmosdb / databaseAccounts group refers to Cosmos DB accounts (the RU/serverless Cosmos model).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services are under Microsoft.DocumentDB historically in docs, and older Cosmos DB workflows use az cosmosdb; the model returned the older Cosmos CLI group rather than the documentdb mongocluster commands introduced for the vCore service.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb documentation / databaseAccounts pages (Cosmos DB)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used az cosmosdb commands, they would target a different (Cosmos DB) product or CLI path and fail to manage a mongoClusters resource; CLI samples and README tasks would be incorrect.
improvements: Update any agent-kit quickstarts to list the exact CLI group candidates and include example az documentdb mongocluster create commands when the target is an Azure DocumentDB (vCore) cluster.
Add a short diagnostic note in the `documentdb-mcp-setup` skill that says: "If you see az cosmosdb examples in older docs, don't use them for vCore clusters; use az documentdb mongocluster instead."

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (...). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters deploy with the ARM/Bicep resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples and API versions exist in Learn). Terraform usages target the mongoClusters resource (or use AzAPI / AVM modules for DocumentDB mongoClusters) rather than azurerm_cosmosdb_account which is for Cosmos databaseAccounts.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM/Terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource is close in name and in the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider namespace; the cold answer reflects the older Cosmos DB Terraform/Bicep resources rather than the newer mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account in example IaC would deploy a different service and produce either a provisioning error or a cluster that doesn't match the vCore DocumentDB expected (the sample would then target the wrong API).
improvements: On the 'Deploy' docs and the agent kit's `documentdb-azure-deployment` skill, add a clear mapping table: 'use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore DocumentDB; use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB (RU)'.
Include a Bicep snippet in the skill that shows the minimal mongoClusters resource example and label it 'vCore DocumentDB — use this for mongoClusters'.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for Cosmos DB: use mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Non-SRV example (TLS port): mongodb://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&appName=@<account>@ ... host suffix *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and TLS port commonly 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (vCore mongoClusters) the connection strings are returned by the cluster (e.g., mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/ ...). Clusters support SRV connection strings and, when 'query-from-any-node' is used, the cluster may expose per-node ports starting at 10260 for node endpoints (gateway/local dev uses 10260). The older pattern using *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255 describes Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) rather than the vCore mongoClusters service.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings / Quickstart connection guidance
Query from any node (ports starting at 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The connection-string host suffix and port differ between the older Cosmos DB Mongo API and the newer DocumentDB mongoClusters; the cold answer mixed the Cosmos host pattern and port (10255) into the vCore product.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the wrong host suffix / port pattern (10255 and *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com) they may not be able to connect to the cluster or would build client code with incorrect connection hints; the correct approach is to get the cluster's connection string (mongodb+srv) and respect its ports (and query-from-any-node port ranges when relevant).
improvements: Add a short 'Which connection string to use' note on the quickstart pages that shows both the mongoClusters SRV format and contrasts it explicitly with the older Cosmos DB 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255' pattern.
In the documentdb-mcp-setup skill, include an example of constructing a production connection string for vCore clusters and a separate example showing the Cosmos RU pattern to avoid confusion.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos/DocumentDB is billed in Request Units (RUs) provisioned per database/collection or at account level. There are manual RU/s (fixed), Autoscale RU (auto-scaling of RUs), and a serverless option for small/occasional workloads.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible product) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage. You pick a cluster tier (M10, M20, M30...) that determines vCores and memory; storage volume is billed separately. The RU-based model (Request Units) applies to Azure Cosmos DB's RU/serverless offerings, not the vCore DocumentDB cluster.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute + storage, vCore tiers)
Azure DocumentDB vs Azure Cosmos DB explanation (pricing model distinction)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both offerings are document-store products on Azure and older docs that described Cosmos RU-based billing are easy to conflate with the vCore offering; the model has mixed the two pricing models.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU-based pricing docs (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: If builder assumes RU/s throughput, they might document or attempt to configure RU-based settings (autoscale RUs) that don't exist for a vCore cluster. This affects sample README, guidance on throughput sizing, and any attempt to set throughput programmatically.
improvements: Add a clear 'Pricing and capacity model' section to the top-level quickstarts that differentiates DocumentDB (vCore) vs Cosmos DB (RUs), with one-line definitive statements and links to the appropriate pricing page.
In the documentdb-azure-deployment skill, include an explicit 'do not attempt to set RU/s on a mongoClusters resource; choose tier and storage instead' note.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API the common authentication method is username/password (MongoDB SCRAM-style authentication) where the username includes the account and the password is one of the account keys. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB wire-protocol endpoint — you authenticate with account keys/credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) supports native (SCRAM-style) username/password authentication and also supports Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication / OIDC. Microsoft Entra ID auth is enabled via cluster authConfig (add MicrosoftEntraID to allowedModes) and drivers/clients can use MONGODB-OIDC / OIDC connection string options (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:...).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older or simpler docs and some Cosmos-based quickstarts emphasize SCRAM keys only; the cold answer omitted the newer OIDC/Entra options available for vCore DocumentDB clusters when MicrosoftEntraID is enabled.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID isn't supported they may implement insecure local credentials handling (storing keys unnecessarily) or fail to implement recommended managed-identity/Entra-based auth flows when required by the target environment.
improvements: Add an explicit example in quickstarts showing both SCRAM connection string usage and the OIDC (MONGODB-OIDC) connection string pattern used with Entra IDs, including one small example for Visual Studio Code / Compass and one for driver-initiated OIDC flows.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., npm package mongodb for Node.js). Do not use the Cosmos DB SQL (azure-cosmos) SDK when talking to the MongoDB wire protocol; use the MongoDB driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — applications should use the official MongoDB drivers for the language (e.g., the npm 'mongodb' driver for Node.js) when connecting to Azure DocumentDB's MongoDB wire-protocol endpoint. There is no separate service-specific Mongo SDK for the data plane; the standard MongoDB drivers are the right choice.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: n/a

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: As I understand Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not natively provide built-in vector indexes (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) like specialized vector DBs. There is no Cosmos-specific createVectorIndex command in the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect. Azure DocumentDB includes an integrated vector store and supports multiple vector index kinds (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann). Vector indexes are created using collection index creation (createIndexes/createIndex) with a cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions payload (e.g., specifying kind:'vector-hnsw' or 'vector-diskann' and parameters such as dimensions, m, efConstruction, numLists). Vector search is then done via the $search aggregation stage and cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector search docs, examples)
Example using an HNSW index

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Vector features are newer and not universally supported across all Azure document-store products; the model defaulted to 'no vector support' as older docs for Cosmos Mongo API lacked an integrated vector store.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed vectors are unavailable they would avoid showing the integrated vector features (index creation and $search queries) that are available and useful in the sample environment; conversely, if they used a vector command meant for another product, it would fail.
improvements: Prominently advertise vector support and example createIndex payloads on the 'Quickstart: Vector search' pages and add a short 'vector index examples' snippet into the documentdb-indexing skill.
Add a small sample in the Node.js quickstart that shows creating a vector index and running a $search so sample repos can optionally include RAG demos.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search is not a first-class built-in feature of Cosmos DB's MongoDB API. Typical approach is to index documents into Azure Cognitive Search ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports integrated full-text and hybrid search via the createSearchIndexes / $search aggregation stage (BM25) and supports combining lexical and vector retrieval (hybrid) via the cosmosSearch operator. While some earlier Cosmos or Cosmos-Mongo docs required external Azure Cognitive Search, the vCore DocumentDB offers built-in $search and createSearchIndexes capabilities.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search with createSearchIndexes and $search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical guidance for Cosmos DB sometimes recommended Azure Cognitive Search for advanced text features; newer DocumentDB integrates full-text (BM25) and hybrid search features, which the cold answer overlooked.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder treats full-text as external-only they'll add needless external dependencies and miss the sample's opportunity to show $search or hybrid queries, or may present outdated migration guidance.
improvements: Add a 'Full-text and Hybrid Search' quick example into the Node.js quickstart that uses createSearchIndexes and $search so samples demonstrate the built-in capability.
Update any agent kit pages implying that full-text requires Cognitive Search; clarify where external search is still recommended and where integrated $search suffices.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API has supported a limited subset of MongoDB server versions (common supported compatibility targets in the past were 3.6 and 4.0, newer accounts added support for later compatibility levels incrementally). Not all MongoDB features are supported: server-side JavaScript (db.eval), some aggregation operators, some admin commands, and certain storage-engine specific behaviors may be missing or behave differently.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) supports modern MongoDB wire protocol/server versions — documentation lists support for MongoDB 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 compatibility targets. Many MongoDB features are supported (99.03% of operators as published), but some admin/diagnostic commands differ and a small set of operators may not be supported; always run a compatibility assessment before migration.

grounding_links.title: Migrate and compatibility notes; supported MongoDB wire protocol versions
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled older limitations of Cosmos DB's Mongo API; the vCore DocumentDB product has broader (and newer) MongoDB protocol/version support and different compatibility characteristics.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed an older compatibility level they might unnecessarily avoid modern driver features and newer aggregation operators, degrading sample quality or causing unnecessary shims.
improvements: Add a short compatibility table on top-level docs that lists the exact MongoDB wire protocol versions supported (5.0..8.0), and link to the compatibility assessment tool for migration validation.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a Cosmos DB Emulator for the Cosmos SQL (Core) API; historically the emulator does NOT fully support the MongoDB API. For local development against a MongoDB-compatible interface use a local MongoDB server (Docker image mongo:latest) on the standard MongoDB port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which serves the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The Cosmos DB emulator is for the SQL/Core API and historically lacks full MongoDB API parity; using a local DocumentDB gateway image (port 10260) is the recommended dev path.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed up the Cosmos DB emulator limitations and generic advice to use local MongoDB; DocumentDB provides a recommended Gateway image and a specific port (10260) for local dev that the cold answer missed.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Core API) does not fully support MongoDB API

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used mongod:latest on 27017 instead of the DocumentDB gateway they might miss DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, integrated search) or experience parity differences; but running against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) is acceptable per the sample requirements.
improvements: Make the local-deployment 'Gateway image on 10260' recommendation more prominent on the quickstart and on the documentdb-local-deployment skill so agents don't default to plain mongo:latest.
Add a ready-made docker-compose snippet (in the skill or quickstart) that binds 10260 for Mongo and documents required TLS flags.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes a change feed concept in the Core API. The MongoDB API historically did not provide full native MongoDB change streams in all compatibility versions; behavior differs. If you need document-change notifications you should use Cosmos DB change feed or the management/diagnostic tools that integrate with it. For MongoDB drivers, watch() support may be limited or unavailable depending on the compatibility version.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams for the MongoDB API. Drivers can use the standard change stream API (collection.watch()) and the service offers resumable streams (resumeAfter, startAtOperationTime) and an integrated change-stream feature — in some contexts you may need to enable the change-stream feature on the cluster or ensure sufficient log retention/time window for historical replay. Documentation includes examples and notes about feature enablement.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (watch(), resume tokens, historical checkpoints)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Earlier Cosmos/Mongo compatibility incarnations had incomplete change-stream support; the cold answer reflected older constraints rather than the current vCore DocumentDB change-stream capabilities.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams aren't available they'd implement a polling solution or use the Cosmos Core change feed approach — both are more complex or less direct than using watch() where supported.
improvements: Make the 'enable change streams' step explicit in cluster quickstarts and in the azure-deployment skill, including the exact CLI/Bicep snippet to toggle authConfig/feature gate so agents can programmatically validate the cluster is change-stream-enabled.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile for data-plane inspection and tools specific to Cosmos/DocumentDB. The generic Azure MCP server (for Azure Resource Manager) covers provisioning and management but the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane helpers (indexes/collections/query plans) for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server supplies data-plane tools for indexes, queries, explain, list databases/collections and should be used for data-plane operations; the general Azure MCP server (azure) covers control-plane tasks but not DocumentDB data-plane queries and index management.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-mcp-setup

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: n/a

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for the service that was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the Core/SQL API). Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's globally distributed, multi-model database service. It is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB and also distinct from AWS DocumentDB (Amazon DocumentDB is an AWS service).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly true but ambiguous: the brand 'DocumentDB' has been used several ways. The current vCore product is named Azure DocumentDB (a vCore MongoDB-compatible service) and was earlier presented as the vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB. Separately, the older 'DocumentDB' name (2014) evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (Core/SQL API). Also there is an open-source DocumentDB engine project that powers the vCore service. The relationships are nuanced: the new Azure DocumentDB product is distinct from Cosmos DB's RU model and from Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Why migrate to Azure DocumentDB (product history & relationship to Cosmos DB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical rebrandings and reuse of the 'DocumentDB' name across Azure products (2014 DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; then 'vCore Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' → 'Azure DocumentDB') create ambiguity and cause simple summaries to be imprecise.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation in the sample could mislead users about which service the sample targets (vCore DocumentDB vs Cosmos RU).
improvements: Create a short 'naming timeline' note on the main overview page that clarifies: (a) the 2014 DocumentDB (later Cosmos DB Core/SQL), (b) Cosmos DB RU-based MongoDB API (databaseAccounts), and (c) the vCore 'Azure DocumentDB' (mongoClusters) and how they differ.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB uses Microsoft's proprietary storage and query engine; for the MongoDB API it implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of its engine. Application code should use MongoDB drivers and standard MongoDB APIs but be aware of behavioral differences and unsupported MongoDB features (so some server-side features or admin commands may not work exactly like a native MongoDB server).
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore Azure DocumentDB product the engine is the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed under MIT / Linux Foundation) built on PostgreSQL; the service implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of that engine. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers, but there are small behavioral differences and a compatibility assessment is recommended before migration.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB engine and compatibility (open-source DocumentDB engine)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's historically-proprietary engine and not the vCore DocumentDB product's open-source DocumentDB engine; the two are easy to conflate because of overlapping names.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a proprietary engine they might over- or under-estimate migration constraints and licensing concerns — this affects migration guidance but not the sample code, which should still use MongoDB drivers.
improvements: Add a short 'engine and license' blurb in the quickstart explaining the open-source DocumentDB engine and its implications, plus link to the GitHub repo for the open-source engine.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for composite unique deduplication on (customerId, eventId)?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a compound unique index on (customerId, eventId): db.events.createIndex({ customerId: 1, eventId: 1 }, { unique: true, name: 'customer_event_unique' })
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — create a compound unique index on customerId and eventId using createIndex with the unique option (e.g., db.events.createIndex({ customerId: 1, eventId: 1 }, { unique: true, name: 'customer_event_unique' })). Note that building a unique index on a populated collection takes a foreground build and may block writes while it builds; plan accordingly.

grounding_links.title: Manage indexing in Azure DocumentDB — compound and unique indexes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: n/a

confusions.question: Which MongoDB API call should the Node.js ingestion service use for high-throughput unordered bulk writes?
confusions.cold_answer: Use collection.bulkWrite(operationsArray, { ordered: false }) from the official mongodb Node.js driver (or use bulk operations API like initializeUnorderedBulkOp() in older drivers). Example: await collection.bulkWrite(bulkOps, { ordered: false });
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the official MongoDB Node.js driver's bulkWrite(operations, { ordered: false }) pattern for unordered bulk operations to maximize throughput. DocumentDB supports bulk operations and there are documented batch size limits (max 25,000 writes per single request).

Document size and batch write limits in Azure DocumentDB (max writes per batch 25,000)

confusions.question: How should the sample open a change stream to trigger downstream profile updates?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the MongoDB driver's change stream API: const changeStream = collection.watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); changeStream.on('change', doc => { /* enqueue profile update job */ }); Note: if the target Cosmos account does not support MongoDB-style change streams, use the Cosmos DB change feed mechanism instead.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and actionable: the Node.js driver can open a change stream with collection.watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }) and process change events (or resume). For Azure DocumentDB you may need to ensure the change-stream feature is enabled on the cluster and consider resume tokens and historical checkpoints for reliability.

confusions.question: How must the sample read the connection string and connect (exact Node.js connection code and options)?
confusions.cold_answer: Read from env DOCUMENTDB_URI and connect with MongoClient using TLS and the unified topology. Example: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }); await client.connect(); Use the sample DB name sample_customer_360_02 and do not log the URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct in intent: read the connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and connect with the MongoClient. Use TLS (tls=true) and driver-appropriate modern options; do not log the raw connection string. Use the provided DB name sample_customer_360_02. Prefer current driver options (the modern mongodb driver passes tls:true and driver-specific options rather than legacy useUnifiedTopology flags).

confusions.question: Which database and collection names and throughput expectations should the sample use/create?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_02 and create a collection named events. Ensure the collection has adequate RU/s provisioned for bulk ingest (either provision RUs at collection level or rely on account autoscale); document the RU/s value in the run report. The sample will create the index and then run bulkWrite into sample_customer_360_02.events.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct: use database sample_customer_360_02 and an events collection as requested. However, the throughput wording is wrong for the vCore DocumentDB product: capacity is provisioned by cluster tier (vCores) and storage, not by RUs; the sample should document cluster tier and storage sizing rather than RU/s.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the sample's requested DB/collection names (correct) with the older Cosmos RU-based throughput model (incorrect for vCore).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder documents RU/s tuning instructions they will mislead readers and create irrelevant steps; the sample should instead note the cluster tier (e.g., M30) and document any cluster-level sizing assumptions.
improvements: In the sample README, state 'database: sample_customer_360_02; collection: events; cluster tier: M30 (as provided) — DocumentDB uses compute tiers (vCores) and storage, not RUs.' and link to the pricing doc.

information_gaps.title: Recommended Node mongodb driver version for Node 24 and MongoDB 7.0
information_gaps.description: Microsoft docs recommend using the official MongoDB driver but do not pin a single recommended npm driver version for Node 24 + MongoDB 7.0 compatibility. The builder needs a recommended major driver version to pin in package.json and to record in the sample. I searched Microsoft Learn quickstarts and compatibility docs but found no single recommended NPM version string for Node 24.

information_gaps.title: Default batch sizing guidance for unordered bulkWrite on M30
information_gaps.description: While docs state absolute max writes per batch (25,000) and that unordered bulkWrite is supported, there is no prescriptive recommendation for a default batch size / memory target and flush interval that balances latency and cluster resource consumption for an M30 tier ingest workload. I searched the performance/bulk-write docs and index guidance but found tuning heuristics only for vector indexes and general batch limits.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb) when you reference or show cluster provisioning or management; see the mongoClusters docs for Bicep/CLI examples.
Do not refer to Request Units (RUs) for sizing the sample cluster — document sizing in terms of cluster tier (vCores, e.g., M30) and storage. See the DocumentDB pricing and compute docs for guidance.

Read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (env) and connect with the official MongoDB Node.js driver; do not log secrets. If Microsoft Entra ID/OIDC is required, use the MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism pattern after enabling MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster.
